title: Provide guidance and address production, healthcare and biosecurity problems on a poultry farm, at

lessons.title: Spotting and solving production and health problems
lessons.html:
The team leader's role

As a team leader or senior worker, you are often the first person to notice that something is wrong in a poultry house. Your job is to spot problems early, take the first steps to fix them, guide the workers and report to the supervisor or manager.

Common production problems and first checks

ProblemFirst things to check
Birds not drinkingWater pressure, blocked nipples, empty tank, line height, water too warm
Feed intake downEmpty feeders, auger fault, feed quality, house too hot, sick birds
Uneven growthFeeder and drinker space, brooding temperature, chick quality, uneven spread
Egg numbers droppingLight timer, water, feed, heat stress, disease, stress from handling
Wet litterLeaking drinkers, poor ventilation, high stocking, diarrhoea

Health problems

Watch for the warning signs: more deaths than normal, birds sitting with ruffled feathers, coughing or rattling breathing, swollen heads, diarrhoea, or a sudden drop in water and feed use. When you see these:

  1. Tell the supervisor immediately and give the facts: house number, number of dead birds, signs seen.
  2. Keep a few fresh dead birds cool for the vet if your supervisor asks, in a sealed bag.
  3. Stop movement of people and equipment from that house to other houses.
  4. Record the signs and times on the house sheet.

Sudden high deaths with swollen heads or breathing signs could be avian influenza or Newcastle disease. These must be reported to the state vet under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984. Your manager will do this, but your quick report is what starts it.

Thinking it through

Use a simple method: what is the problem, when did it start, where is it (one house or all), how many birds, and what changed? Often the answer is a simple thing like a blocked water filter or a broken fan. Fix what you are allowed to fix, and report the rest.

lessons.title: Guiding workers on good practice and biosecurity
lessons.html:
Showing, not only telling

Workers learn best when you show them the right way and then watch them do it. As a team leader you guide workers every day on how to care for the birds and keep biosecurity strong.

How to guide a worker

  1. Explain the task and why it matters. For example: we clean drinkers daily because dirty water spreads germs.
  2. Show the task step by step.
  3. Let the worker do it while you watch.
  4. Praise what is right and correct what is wrong, kindly and clearly.
  5. Check again later in the day.

Fixing biosecurity problems

Biosecurity fails when people take short cuts. Common problems you must correct:

  • Workers skipping the footbath or the footbath water being dirty or empty.
  • Doors left open, letting wild birds and rats in.
  • Tools and buckets moved between houses without cleaning.
  • Visitors entering without signing the register or changing clothes.
  • Feed spills left on the ground.
  • Dead birds left in the house or near the gate.

When you see a short cut, stop it at once and explain why. If it keeps happening, report it to the supervisor. Biosecurity protects the farm and everyone's jobs.

Health and safety guidance

Remind workers to wear dust masks, gloves and boots, to wash hands before eating, and to follow the label when mixing disinfectants. Never let workers mix chemicals together unless the label says so. Report any injury straight away.

Communicating with the supervisor

Give short, clear reports: what you found, what you did and what still needs doing. Write it in the daily record so the next shift knows.

Key points

  • Spot problems early and check simple causes like water, feed and fans first.
  • Report rising deaths or disease signs immediately with clear facts.
  • Stop movement from a house with suspected disease.
  • Guide workers by explaining, showing, watching and checking.
  • Correct biosecurity short cuts at once and explain why.
